hops.afterHeading: Three polymers built for different jobs
hops.title: Bend one wet hair, then stretch it
hops.text: Find a fallen hair on a brush or sweater; no plucking. Push its two ends toward each other and it buckles at the slightest touch. Now wet it under the tap, pinch one end between the thumb and finger of each hand, and pull slowly. The same strand that folded so easily holds on. Its cortex is packed with keratin intermediate filaments. In lab tests on horse tail hairs stretched in water, the keratin coiled coils began to unravel at about 5 percent stretch and formed beta-sheets above about 20 percent. In a separate test, a human hair broke at about 1.6 times its starting length.

sources.citation: Kreplak, L., Doucet, J., Dumas, P., & Briki, F. (2004). New aspects of the alpha-helix to beta-sheet transition in stretched hard alpha-keratin fibers. Biophys. J., 87(1), 640-647.
Paschou, A. M., et al. (2026). A Raman spectroscopy investigation of the resilience of hair cuticular scales under uniaxial stress. J. Mech. Behav. Biomed. Mater., 178, 107391.
Takajo, D. (2026). Mechanocaloric effect of human hair. J. Mech. Behav. Biomed. Mater., 178, 107412.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Illustration of two hands over a sink, pinching the ends of one wet hair and pulling it gently taut.
image.caption: A wet hair buckles at a touch, yet its keratin filaments let it stretch far before snapping.

hops.afterHeading: One end: the doorway and its critical concentration
hops.title: Antarctic fish microtubules that assemble at −1.8 °C
hops.text: Chill mammalian microtubules toward freezing and they come apart. Yet the Antarctic fish Pagothenia borchgrevinki lives in seawater at −1.8 °C. In 1985, biochemists found that its purified tubulin, in a lab buffer at that temperature, had a critical concentration of about 0.74 milligrams per millilitre. Mammalian tubulin, they reckoned, would need at least a hundred times more. They found no sign of a helper factor; the change is in the tubulin. In related fishes, a handful of amino-acid swaps on the sides and in the cores of α- and β-tubulin are thought to favor assembly. In the lab, their microtubules grow and shrink more slowly than warm mammalian ones.

sources.citation: Williams, R. C. Jr., Correia, J. J., & DeVries, A. L. (1985). Formation of microtubules at low temperature by tubulin from antarctic fish. Biochemistry, 24(11), 2790-2798.
Detrich, H. W. 3rd, Parker, S. K., Williams, R. C. Jr., Nogales, E., & Downing, K. H. (2000). Cold adaptation of microtubule assembly and dynamics. J. Biol. Chem., 275(47), 37038-37047.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Illustration of a small dark fish swimming beneath blue sea ice in icy water.
image.caption: Antarctic fish tubulin keeps a low critical concentration at −1.8 °C, with no helper protein.

hops.afterHeading: Two ends: why hydrolysis makes them differ
hops.title: How Listeria rides host actin from cell to cell
hops.text: Listeria monocytogenes can spread between macrophages without ever leaving the inside of a cell, out of reach of antibodies. In 1989, electron micrographs of infected macrophages showed bacteria trailing 'comet tails' of host actin, often about 5 micrometres long. The tail drives the bacterium into a finger of membrane, and a neighboring macrophage swallows the finger whole. In 1992, the same lab found that new filaments the bacterium starts have their barbed ends at its surface. In detergent-opened infected macrophages given actin below the pointed end's critical concentration, filaments still grew at those barbed ends. Given fresh actin, bacteria moved away from their old tails as those filaments lengthened.

sources.citation: Tilney, L. G., & Portnoy, D. A. (1989). Actin filaments and the growth, movement, and spread of the intracellular bacterial parasite, Listeria monocytogenes. J. Cell Biol., 109(4), 1597-1608.
Tilney, L. G., DeRosier, D. J., Weber, A., & Tilney, M. S. (1992). How Listeria exploits host cell actin to form its own cytoskeleton. II. J. Cell Biol., 118(1), 83-93.

image.caption: Host actin adds subunits at barbed ends against Listeria's surface, pushing it into the next cell.
